relationship_to_restored_text: Interpretive contemplative layer aligned by verse. This does not replace the source-audited restored translation.

verses.mystical_translation: Thirty-two allied kings surround Samaria with horses, chariots, and siege.
Ben-hadad sends demands into the enclosed city.
He claims Ahab's wealth, wives, and children as the victor's property.
Ahab initially yields himself and everyone attached to him.
The conqueror repeats the demand.
Then he expands it into a house-by-house search and seizure.
Ahab finally consults elders, admitting he had not withheld even his family.
The people tell the king not to consent.
Ahab draws a boundary at the second demand.
Ben-hadad answers with an oath of overwhelming destruction.
Ahab warns that the person putting on armor should not boast as though battle were over.
The besieging coalition moves into formation from its drinking shelters.
A prophet promises the great force will be given into Ahab's hand.
Young provincial attendants are selected to open the battle under Ahab's command.
A small force is counted against the coalition.
They emerge at noon while the allied kings are intoxicated.
The first young fighters become the objects of enemy observation.
Ben-hadad orders them captured alive whether they seek peace or war.
The attendants step out with the army behind them.
Close combat becomes rout, and Ben-hadad escapes by horse.
Israel destroys horses, chariots, and many Aramean lives.
The prophet warns that victory has not ended the war.
Aramean advisors explain defeat through geography of the gods.
They replace allied kings with professional governors.
The lost military machine is rebuilt piece for piece.
At the year's return, the army comes to Aphek.
Israel appears like two small goat flocks before a land filled with soldiers.
The next promise answers the claim that YHWH belongs only to mountains.
Seven days of waiting end in a one-day report of enormous slaughter.
A collapsing wall kills thousands more while Ben-hadad hides inside the city.
His servants trust the reputation of Israel's kings for covenant-kindness.
Sackcloth, ropes, and a plea for life reach Ahab, who calls the captive king brother.
The negotiators seize the word of kinship and bring Ben-hadad into Ahab's chariot.
Cities and market rights become terms of a covenant that preserves the defeated king.
A prophet asks a companion to wound him under claimed Divine command.
The refusal is answered by a lion's lethal attack, a terrifying narrative no leader may imitate.
Another person complies and wounds the prophet.
The injury becomes a disguise for confronting Ahab.
A fictional battlefield custody failure is presented to the king.
Ahab pronounces judgment from the man's own story.
The disguise falls, revealing a prophet.
Ahab is condemned for releasing a man marked for destruction, making mercy itself the alleged offense.
The king returns home angry beneath the oracle.

contemplative_note: The chapter asks whether victory requires killing every captive. Its final oracle says yes; an ethical reading must say no. Mercy can coexist with accountability, restitution, and protection. A refusal to assault another person is not spiritual rebellion, and no claimed command should make violence compulsory.
